overviewHtml:
This ungraded knowledge check assesses your understanding of the major responses to the hard problem. You'll be asked about type-A and type-B physicalism, illusionism, panpsychism and the combination problem, Russellian monism, and dualism.

Note: Use this to test yourself, review the feedback on any questions you miss, and retry until you feel confident before moving forward.

forms.stemHtml: What distinguishes type-B physicalism from type-A physicalism?

options.html: Type-B denies that zombies are conceivable
options.text: Type-B denies that zombies are conceivable
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. That's the type-A position. Type-B grants their conceivability.

options.html: Type-B grants a gap in explanation, not in reality
options.text: Type-B grants a gap in explanation, not in reality
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! Type-B holds that experience is physical, though the identity can't be deduced from the physical facts.

options.html: Type-B holds that experience is nonphysical
options.text: Type-B holds that experience is nonphysical
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Both types are physicalist. Type-B holds that experience is identical to physical processes.

options.html: Type-B denies that there are any easy problems
options.text: Type-B denies that there are any easy problems
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Both types accept the easy problems. They differ over the explanatory gap.

options.html: That people have experiences of any kind at all
options.text: That people have experiences of any kind at all
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Illusionists accept that we see, hear, and feel. They aren't denying consciousness.

options.html: That the brain represents its own internal states
options.text: That the brain represents its own internal states
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Illusionism depends on the brain representing its own states, inaccurately.

options.html: That experiences really have phenomenal properties
options.text: That experiences really have phenomenal properties
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! Experiences only seem to have them. The task is to explain that seeming.

options.html: That physics can fully describe the brain's activity
options.text: That physics can fully describe the brain's activity
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Illusionism is a physicalist view.

forms.stemHtml: Which of the following are claims of Russellian monism? (Select all that apply.)

options.html: Physics describes the structure and dynamics of matter
options.text: Physics describes the structure and dynamics of matter
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! It tells us what things do and how they're related.

options.html: Physics doesn't say what matter is intrinsically
options.text: Physics doesn't say what matter is intrinsically
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! Its intrinsic nature is left open.

options.html: Matter's intrinsic nature may be experiential
options.text: Matter's intrinsic nature may be experiential
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! Experience, or its precursors, may fill in the structure physics describes.

options.html: Experience is a separate substance from matter
options.text: Experience is a separate substance from matter
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. That's substance dualism. Russellian monism is a monism.

options.html: Physics already describes everything about experience
options.text: Physics already describes everything about experience
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. On this view, physics describes only structure, not intrinsic nature.

forms.stemHtml: What is the interaction problem for dualism?

options.html: How many small experiences combine into one subject
options.text: How many small experiences combine into one subject
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. That's the combination problem for panpsychism.

options.html: Why phenomenal concepts can't be deduced from physics
options.text: Why phenomenal concepts can't be deduced from physics
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. That's the issue the phenomenal concept strategy addresses.

options.html: How nonphysical experience could affect the physical world
options.text: How nonphysical experience could affect the physical world
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! If physics is causally closed, nonphysical experience seems to have nothing to do.

options.html: Why experiences seem to have phenomenal properties
options.text: Why experiences seem to have phenomenal properties
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. That's the illusion problem.

forms.stemHtml: What is the name for panpsychism's problem of explaining how the experiences of many small entities combine to yield a unified experience such as a human's? Enter two words.

options.feedbackHtml: Correct! Many philosophers regard it as the analogue, for panpsychism, of the hard problem.

forms.defaultFeedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. This is the combination problem.

title: Responses to the Hard Problem
